Posted April 8, 2003
Special Report to MarijuanaNews by Richard Cowan

The refugee hearings for the Kubbys resumed today after a one-month hiatus for Steve to recover from pneumonia. Much stronger, he spent five hours today answering questions from the Immigration Ministry.

Canadian public buildings lack the maximum-security-prison ambience that has come to characterize their DEAland equivalents; nonetheless, they do get down to serious business.

The hearings follow the adversarial model, with the Immigration ministry trying to prove that the Kubbys do not qualify for refugee status. The judge is an Adjudicator and there is also a representative from the Refugee Protection Service. Claimants are responsible for making their own case, however.

Michele Kubby is acting as counsel for Steve, and is doing an excellent job.

There are two reasons for their proceeding without an attorney. First and foremost, they cannot afford the expense. (Steve Tuck is in the same position.) Second, there really are some advantages to representing oneself, in that non-lawyers are allowed more latitude.

The government's case is fairly simple. It maintains that the Kubbys can safely return to DEAland, and they are here as economic refugees that is, because they can enjoy a higher standard of living here. That is not sufficient basis for a refugee claim, or half the people in the world would qualify.

Moreover, Immigration maintains that DEAland is a democratic country in which the accused get due process. It is hardly surprising that they might believe that, and would have to say it, even if they did not believe it. Besides, the Kubby investigation and trial was so bizarre, that Steve repeatedly had to explain what actually happened.

For example, the Immigration lawyer asked Steve about a court appearance at which he was ordered jailed, but the jailer would not take him.
See
 Prosecutor Demands That Kubby Be Jailed to Die Without Medical Marijuana; Judge Agrees, But Jailer Refuses to Commit Murder. Just When You Thought They Couldn't Get Any Crazier

Canada does not want to be in the position of saying that DEAland has become, well, DEAland. However, as I reported on March 5th, they did not flatly state that there could be no such claims by Americans.
See
 Kubby Refugee Hearings Begin. Canadian Government Does Not Assert That There Can Be No Refugees From DEAland. Special to MarijuanaNews.

So they have to argue that Kubby received a fair trial and he could go back to California, probably to the Bay Area, where medical cannabis users are allowed by local authorities to grow the relatively large amounts of cannabis that Steve needs.

There are two literally fatal flaws in that position.

First, Steve Kubby might die within a matter of days if he were to be locked up without cannabis for any reason, and there are large elements of California law enforcement that still refuse to accept Prop 215 and obey state law.
See
 Selective Enforcement Versus Selective Compliance 2 Articles
and
 What Part Of 'Exempt' Do California District Attorneys Still Not Understand?

So he could still end up in a California jail with fatal consequences.

The second problem is that the Feds have three more years to decide whether to prosecute the Kubbys for the cultivation of the plants for which they were acquitted under Prop 215, and there is no medical necessity defense allowed in Federal courts.
See
 Jury Tampering Federal Judge Extorts Guilty Verdict From Terrified Citizens In Major States Rights Case. Rosenthal Conviction Versus the Constitution.

In fact, just today, Lynn and Judy Osborn, charged as suppliers to the Los Angeles club, were told by a Federal judge that they could not make any mention of medical cannabis in their trial.

Even if the Feds chose not to prosecute the Kubbys at this time, they could destroy any medical garden grown by the Kubbys, leaving Steve without his medicine. The Feds have cut down gardens with as few as six plants, but declined to prosecute at this time.

Moreover, they could eventually decide to combine the old charges and any new charges, as they recently did with Steve McWilliams in San Diego, in order to make it appear that Kubby is a commercial grower.
See
 Walters Puts The Media to the Test By Taking Hyper-Lying to A New Level. Blood Libels To Justify Police State. San Diego Medical Activist Faces Federal Charges for 20 Plants.

McWilliams had no choice but to take a plea bargain, even though he had been working with the city.
See
 San Diego Medical Cannabis Activists/Providers Resume Providing Patients with Medicine; Believe It or Not: Meeting with Chief of Police at 4:20 Today.

Patients like Steve Kubby, and Steve Tuck, who need much larger quantities of cannabis than most patients are especially vulnerable. Unless they can afford to pay a hundred dollars per day, or more, they have to grow their own medicine. Even if they don't grow, they are vulnerable to federal prosecution because they will often have to have commercial quantities of cannabis, and could be charged under Federal law, without being able to mention their medical conditions.

Canadian Immigration has no such restrictions, although they are still not quite ready to concede that Steve's life depends on cannabis. This reflects a general ambivalence about the issue.
See
 A Tale of Two Canadas. Debate Over Medical Cannabis Refugees Is A Part of Struggle for National Identity. If They Learn What Has Happened to America, They May Reject That Fate For Themselves.

Steve Tuck points out that they are in similar positions to those who were tried for being witches by being thrown into water. If they were innocent, they would drown.
See
 The Slow Motion Murder of Alan Patriquen. Canada Really Does Have A Death Penalty, But Only for Medical Cannabis Patients. Breaking Their Own Laws To Follow the Prohibitionist Party Line.

The American medical cannabis refugee cases are being closely followed by a local member of the Canadian Parliament, Randy White, who has an interest in immigration laws, and attended the hearings today, and last month.

White is a sincere prohibitionist, but he supports medical cannabis, and very limited decriminalization. We ended up having lunch. We went Dutch, so to speak.

He strongly opposes refugee claims by Americans in general and by medical cannabis patients in particular. He represents an area adjacent to the border and is concerned about DEAland retaliation if Canada goes to far in changing its cannabis laws. And he can't quite bring himself to believe that someone might actually die for lack of cannabis. We are going to talk further.

It is his opinion that these claimants will be denied refugee status, but will not be kicked out of the country. That is sort of the Canadian way of dealing with things.

The hearings resume on Thursday, with testimony by California Judge James Gray, who will presumably talk about the recalcitrance of some elements in California law enforcement, and by Ed Rosenthal, who knows more than he ever wanted to know about Federal policies.

More then.
